title: Exploring How Computers Work
beats: Wonder that a lump of metal and sand follows instructions; presenter admits he is a poor instruction-giver and wants to understand
Literal circuit: one lamp, two switches; light only if both closed
Name the behaviour AND after seeing it; then 0/1 encoding and truth table appear only now
One switch that shorts the lamp: closing it turns light off, hence NOT
Fingers cannot flip switches; electromagnets, tubes, then transistor as an electrically-controlled switch on a breadboard
Abstract the world to two blocks, AND and NOT, in a drag-wire simulator
Wire AND into NOT: build NAND, package it as a chip
Invert inputs into NAND, truth table shows OR; package again (build-up of reusable chips)
Short pointer to Ben Eater and Nand2Tetris as resources
Decimal place value as the familiar, binary is the same rule with two digits; 1101 worked to 13
Add 35+7 by hand column by column, naming sum bit and carry bit
Shrink to two single bits; list the four cases
Carry column equals AND (spotted from the table); sum is almost OR except last row, so patch OR with a NAND, giving XOR
Half adder from XOR plus AND; observe that every column really has three inputs, so add carry-in, second XOR, second AND, OR; test all input classes
Chain four adders by carry wires into a 4-bit adder; test 1+1, 5+1, 7+1; overflow 15+1
Presenter's own wrong belief: top bit is a sign flag; 7 + (-7) does not give 0
Ask what must be added to 7 to get zero; solve bit by bit with carries; -7 is 1001; reinterpret top bit as the -8 place
Count up on the number wheel; odd system but addition just works
Negate = invert then add 1, derived from 'all ones is one short of zero'
Subtract signal: XORs conditionally invert, same signal feeds carry-in; reuse of XOR and carry-in discovered earlier
Call it ALU though it does no logic yet; package it

metrics.key_term: truth table / logic gate (AND, NOT, NAND, XOR) building up to ALU
metrics.misconception: yes: assumed the top bit is a sign flag (12:02), disproved with 7 + (-7)
metrics.brute_force: yes 6:17: 35+7 added by hand in binary before any circuit
metrics.examples: about 8 circuits/tests: AND, NOT, NAND, OR, XOR, half adder, full adder, 4-bit adder, subtract; grow by chip reuse, each test sweeps all input cases
metrics.ending: Modest wrap: ALU packaged, teaser for memory; no recap, no callback to opening wonder

principles.1: confirmed: lamp and switches (0:38) and place-value decimal (5:01) precede every formal idea
principles.2: confirmed: 0/1 table only after AND is seen (1:12); sum and carry bit named only when a worked example needs them (6:34)
principles.3: partly: he wires many chips with the simulator, reuse is shown but the interface is not explicitly taught as a habit
principles.4: confirmed: transistor as finger-switch at 2:03-2:56; switch-to-gate to arithmetic
principles.5: confirmed: paperclip circuit, real breadboard transistor, and hand column addition act out the problem literally
principles.6: confirmed: 35+7 by hand (6:17) is the scratch-pad version that the adder then mechanises
principles.7: confirmed: carry equals AND, sum nearly OR (7:56); negative derivation (12:39); he lets the table show it then names it
principles.8: partly: pace is a steady monologue; new ideas arrive about every 60-90 s, with slower beats in the adder wiring and negatives (more bits-per-idea sections) but no evidence for speech-rate change; transcript cannot show it
principles.9: confirmed: the same test sweep (all off, one on, two on, three on) is repeated for full adder and ALU; chip-and-package loop repeated
principles.10: confirmed: one switch, two switches, two bits, three bits, four bits, ALU
principles.11: confirmed: AND/NOT then NAND, OR, XOR, half adder, full adder, 4-bit adder, negatives, subtract; XOR reused in subtraction
principles.12: partly: points to Ben Eater and Nand2Tetris (4:22) and history from relays to transistors; little else outside
principles.13: partly: plain language and an expert-grade complete build; reasons for tool choice given at each step (why NAND, why XOR, why carry-in), no explicit 12-year-old framing

new_moves.name: truth-table-as-detective-tool
new_moves.what: Write the target's table, then compare columns to chips already owned; match gives a free answer, near-match gives a minimal patch
new_moves.evidence: 7:56-8:29 carry equals AND, sum is OR minus one row, so add NAND

new_moves.name: package-then-reuse
new_moves.what: Each solved circuit is sealed into a named chip so the next level thinks in bigger units

new_moves.name: derive-by-solving-for-the-unknown
new_moves.what: Instead of stating two's complement, ask what number added gives zero and fill in bits right to left

new_moves.name: reinterpret-the-symbol
new_moves.what: Same bit pattern, new weight (-8 place) makes the weird thing make sense

theory: The video teaches by building a tower of reusable named chips where each new chip is found by asking a concrete question of the previous one (what table am I missing? what must be added to get zero?) and then verified immediately in the simulator. Vocabulary arrives after the behaviour is visible, and presenter fallibility (his sign-bit mistake) makes the discovery feel like shared work.
velocity: Scene builder: support 'package as chip' so solved sub-circuits become single labelled blocks in later scenes
Orchestrator: before naming a concept, show the behaviour and its table, then attach the label
Evals: after any build step, auto-run an exhaustive input sweep and show it on screen
Learner model: log which chips a learner has built so later playbooks can say 'use the XOR you made'
Voice: model a wrong prior belief (sign bit) and let the simulation refute it
quote: only light up if both inputs are on
